statement.p: Use the figure below to estimate the indicated derivatives. If a derivative does not exist, enter dne in the answer blank. The graph of f(x) is black and has a sharp corner at x = 2. The graph of g(x) is blue.

solution.p: Using the quotient rule, we know that j'(x) = (g'(x) \cdot f(x) - g(x) \cdot f'(x))/(f(x))^2. We use slope to compute the derivatives. Since f(x) is linear on the interval 0 \lt x \lt 2, we compute the slope of the line to see that f'(x) = 1 on this interval. Similarly, we compute the slope on the interval 2 \lt x \lt 4 to see that f'(x) = -1 on that interval. Since f(x) has a corner at x = 2, we know that f'(2) does not exist. Similarly, g(x) is linear on the interval shown, and we see that the slope of g(x) on this interval is -0.75 so we have g'(x) = -0.75 on this interval.

B. We have j'(2) = (g'(2) \cdot f(2) - g(2) \cdot f'(2))/(f(2)^2). Since f(x) has a corner at x = 2 we know that f'(2) does not exist. This results in the derivative of the quotient j(x) not existing at this point, as suggested by the quotient rule given here, and thus j'(2) does not exist.
